items.title: South Central 102: How Deutsche Bank enabled money laundering and sanctioned oligarchs
items.summary: Can a global banking giant like Deutsche Bank be held accountable for allegedly enabling money laundering and hiding sanctioned oligarchs? What do 15.5 million leaked Deutsche Bank documents reveal about the bank’s role in the global financial system? In this week’s South Central, hosts Dhanya Rajendran and Pooja Prasanna examine a major international investigation into Deutsche Bank. They are joined by investigative journalist Josy Joseph, who led the investigation against Deutsche Bank. The investigation is based on approximately 15.5 million internal documents. Josy explains how the documents point to Deutsche Bank’s role in enabling sanctioned oligarchs to conceal their wealth and facilitating large-scale money laundering. He describes the bank as one of the central pieces of infrastructure in the global financial system, with its operations and correspondent banking networks spanning countries across the world. The conversation explores how financial institutions are supposed to identify suspicious transactions, why red flags can be overlooked, and how the pursuit of profit can take precedence over compliance. Joseph explains how internal alerts and anti-money laundering checks can be overridden when business interests take priority. Josy also discusses some of the stories emerging from the investigation, including money-laundering schemes with Russian connections, transactions linked to the Trump family, and money routed through Deutsche Bank to Israel amid the war in Gaza. He says the team is only beginning to uncover what lies within the millions of documents, with more stories, including those connected to South Asia, still to emerge. In the second part of the episode, the hosts turn to the growing number of social media posts being taken down following government requests. In Kerala alone, 15,000 posts have been removed from social media since the UDF came to power in May 2026, according to a figure presented by a minister in the state Assembly. The conversation also discusses takedown requests reported in other states. They are joined by lawyer Nikhil Narendran, to explain how government-ordered content removals work, the legal provisions being used, and what this means for freedom of expression online. The discussion also examines the lack of transparency around takedown requests, the absence of an effective appeals process for users, and the implications for journalists, independent media and ordinary social media users. items.title: After 4 decades of political cartoons, Cartoonists Combine restricted on Insta in India
items.summary: An organisation born of the legacy of one of India’s best-known political cartoonists now finds its digital platform restricted. Cartoonists Combine is a collective that has spent over four decades bringing together artists and represents more than 100 cartoonists in Maharashtra. It was founded in 1983 on the initiative of Balasaheb Thackeray, himself a political cartoonist. But at 2 am on November 20, Instagram temporarily restricted the collective’s account in India. Gaurav Sarjerao, president of the collective, said an Instagram notification on November 19 – restricting access to a post in India – had warned that the account could be restricted “if you continue to share such content”. That post had contained a cartoon depicting PM Modi as a king whose life depended on a parrot, with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar portrayed as the parrot. “I am not sure whether the account was taken down because of that particular cartoon, but we did receive a notification regarding it,” said Sarjerao. The notification mentioned the restriction came after a request from the government or law enforcement agency under section 73(b) of the Information Technology Act. Newslaundry has reached out to Meta India to ask about the agency involved and the details of the request. This report will be updated if a response is received. Sarjerao said the collective will now raise objections, “protest and fight” for the account to be fully restored. Rohit Kabade, a cartoonist associated with the collective, said the last cartoon posted before the restriction, also on November 19, was titled “Lapocracy”. He had made it in response to Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma’s comments after the launch of Sonia Gandhi's book, which related to Rahul Gandhi’s remarks about his mother sitting on his father’s lap during meals. The cartoon shows Sarma on Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s lap, while Modi sits on the lap of businessman Gautam Adani. Cartoons were usually posted by the collective’s Instagram account in collaboration with the artists. items.title: Plea in Supreme Court to prevent turncoat MPs, MLAs from resigning to evade anti-defection law

[A Sethu v. Union of India & Ors.] A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana sought responses from the Election Commission of India, Law Commission of India, Ministry of Law and Justice and Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs on the petition filed by A Sethu. According to the petition, strategically timed resignations, coupled with delays in deciding disqualification petitions, allow legislators to avoid the consequences of alleged defection and undermine the electoral mandate. “A resignation process that can be used to postpone, and then to avoid, the consequences of defection, coupled with the absence of any enforced time-limit for deciding disqualification petitions, impairs the integrity of the electoral mandate…By the time a petition is decided, or a Court is approached, the term of the House may have run, the by-election may have been held, and the Government may have fallen or survived,” the petition said. items.title: New Supreme Court Bench trims scope of pan-India unauthorised construction case
items.summary: A new Supreme Court bench on Monday reduced the scope of the case on unauthorised construction and residential land misuse across India [ Loganathan vs. State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. ]. The case was recently reassigned to the present bench of Justices BV Nagarathna and Sanjeev Sachdeva from a bench led by Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah. The bench of Justice Amanullah had taken up the exercise of violations of building laws across India despite the individual case before it having been disposed off. This had led to a spate of new petitions and applications before the Court. When the matter came up before the bench of Justices Nagarathna and Sachdeva today, the Court observed that a dismissed appeal cannot be turned into an open-ended forum for settling disputes across the country. Accordingly, the bench disposed of all pending intervention and individual applications, granting liberty to affected parties to approach local municipal authorities, statutory tribunals, or their respective High Courts. Justice BV Nagarathna and Justice Sanjeev Sachdeva In a detailed order, the Bench said that it was neither practical nor feasible for the apex court to monitor building bye-law breaches statewide or case-by-case. It added that the pendency of the matter had triggered a proliferation of writ petitions and applications seeking private relief. "All pending applications before this Court seeking whatever relief may be are disposed of with liberty to the parties to approach the concerned authorities, municipal corporations or municipalities, tribunals or the High Court in the respective States," the Court ordered. The Court limited the case strictly to seeking suggestions from State governments and Union Territories on how to curb building bye-law violations and strengthen municipal enforcement. It ordered the authorities to file affidavits offering concrete suggestions on enforcing building regulations and preventing unauthorised constructions. items.title: You have a good case: Supreme Court issues notice on bail petition despite POCSO accused wanting to withdraw case
items.summary: In an unusual turn of events, Supreme Court on Monday refused to allow a lawyer to withdraw a bail petition filed on behalf of an accused booked under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act (POCSO Act). The Court instead chose to seek the State's response after noting that the underlying relationship between the accused and victim appeared to be consensual. The order issuing notice was passed by Justices JB Pardiwala and Vinod K Chandran when the petitioner's counsel sought to pull out of the proceedings. As soon as the matter was called, the advocate informed the Bench that she had instructions from her client to withdraw the petition with liberty to approach the trial court for bail. Taken aback by the request, Justice Pardiwala asked why the petitioner was backing out when she appeared to have a strong case on merits. "Why are you withdrawing?" Justice Pardiwala asked. "With liberty to approach the trial court for bail," the counsel replied. "Why? You don't have a good case? You are praying for bail? Who has instructed you to withdraw?" the judge pressed further. Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice Vinod Chandran When the advocate clarified that the instructions had come directly from her client, Justice Chandran stepped in and asked whether the lawyer would object if the Court went ahead and issued notice anyway. "Will you have an objection if we issue notice? You have a good case," Justice Chandran remarked, observing that "their affair seems to be consensual." "Very strange client. Issue notice," Justice Pardiwala said, ordering notice to be issued to the State rather than dismissing the petition as withdrawn. As the relieved junior counsel thanked the Bench, saying she was "extremely grateful," Justice Pardiwala quipped: "We have not yet granted you (bail)."

items.title: ITAT quashes ₹140 crore tax additions against Hero MotoCorp Chairman Pawan Munjal
items.summary: The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) at Delhi has quashed tax reassessment proceedings initiated against Hero MotoCorp Chairman and Managing Director Pawan Munjal with respect to additions of ₹140.70 crore to his taxable income for assessment year 2017-18. In a judgment delivered on November 20, a bench of Vice President Mahavir Singh and Accountant Member S Rifaur Rahman held that the reassessment order was barred by limitation since it was dispatched after the statutory deadline. The tribunal also rejected the Income Tax Department's allegations concerning unexplained investments in land and personal expenditure incurred by Hero MotoCorp. " If the Department’s contention were accepted, an order could be prepared, dated and retained internally within the Department on the last date of limitation, but issued to the assessee at any later date. Such an interpretation would defeat the object of prescribing a definite period for completion of reassessment proceedings, " the verdict said. Hence, it set aside the tax additions. The dispute arose from searches conducted against Hero MotoCorp and individuals associated with the group in March 2022. Following the searches, the Department reopened Munjal's assessments and made additions of ₹35.28 crore towards alleged unexplained investment in land at Chhatarpur in Delhi and ₹105.41 crore towards alleged personal expenditure incurred by the company. The Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) subsequently deleted the land-related addition and reduced the personal expenditure addition to ₹26.14 crore. Both sides challenged the decision before the ITAT. The tribunal noted that although the reassessment order was dated March 31, 2024, it was dispatched only on April 1 after the statutory deadline had expired. It held that merely dating an order within the limitation period was insufficient when its actual dispatch occurred subsequently. Regarding the merits of the allegations, the tribunal found no evidence establishing that Munjal had paid undisclosed cash consideration for the land. It held that documents recovered from third parties, without corroborative evidence connecting Munjal to the alleged payments, could not justify additions towards unexplained investments. Regarding personal expenditure, the tribunal ruled that disallowance of business expenses in an employer's assessment did not automatically make those expenses taxable benefits in the employee's hands. items.title: Technology can undermine justice if poorly designed: Delhi High Court Justice Tejas Karia
items.summary: Technology, if poorly designed, can cause more harm than good in India's justice system, said Delhi High Court judge Justice Tejas Karia on Sunday. Justice Karia was speaking at the inaugural edition of JusTech, a national conclave organised by the Dharmashastra National Law University. Jabalpur (DNLU). His address focused on addressing the justice gap by harnessing technology. He pointed out that the justice gap does not arise because of any lacunae in law, but due to various barriers such as cost, accessibility, complexity, undue delays, and a lack of trust in the system. Justice Karia opined that Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) can be a handy tool to bridge the gap, without replacing human involvement. " Mediation is the norm of the day. We all know that mediation is very valuable, but if it can be done in online mode, what all it can achieve: all the barriers which we just discussed can be easily eliminated with the help of an Online Dispute Resolution mechanism. ODR doesn't mean they are replacing judges with computers, or that they are removing the human aspect of it. ODR, or Online Dispute Resolution, is only providing a tool. And it can be a tool by which the documents can be exchanged, there can be video conferencing, you can have the platforms where you can have negotiations, and also sometimes an early determination or an expert determination can also be done through the ODR mechanism ," he said. He pointed out that ODR reduces the need for litigants to incur travel expenses or miss days of work and enables them to approach cases from the comfort and familiarity of their homes. AI tools could also reduce the burden on courts by automatically grouping similar cases. However, he warned that for the benefits of technology to truly percolate the justice system, there must be strong safeguards in place. " Technology can improve justice, but it can also undermine it if poorly designed, and an ODR system must never come as a result of a fast lane for an unfair outcome ," he said. The judge went on to suggest various safeguards to bear in mind while using technolgy in the administration of justice. Key principles outlined by him in this regard include equal bargaining power among stakeholders, impartiality of the decision-maker, whether arbitrator, mediator, or algorithm, robust cybersecurity to protect personal data, informed consent rather than blind compliance, and continuous human oversight. items.title: Punjab & Haryana High Court denies anticipatory bail to man accused of stealing his own vehicle from police station
items.summary: The Punjab and Haryana High Court recently denied anticipatory bail to a man accused of stealing his own vehicle from a police station in Hisar last month [ Dharmender Dudi alias Dharmender alias Mahender Dharamender Dudi v State of Haryana ]. The vehicle had been impounded after the driver was allegedly found driving while intoxicated. Justice Vikram Aggarwal declined to consider the driver's claim that his vehicle was taken away by the police as he did not succumb to their monetary demands. The judge said the accused had committed a serious offence by allegedly stealing the impounded car from the premises of the police station. "It indeed is a very serious offence where the petitioner dared to commit a theft in the police station. This Court is not inclined to go into the version of the petitioner at this stage that he was intentionally issued challans and that his vehicle was taken away since he did not succumb to monetary demands. These allegations do not outweigh the allegations in the FIR," the Court said. Justice Vikram Aggarwal The petitioner, Dharmender Dudi, had approached the Court seeking anticipatory bail in a case registered against him at Azad Nagar Police Station in Hisar district under Sections 305 and 331(4) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which deal with theft and house-trespass, respectively. His counsel said he was issued challans on October 1 and his car was also taken from his farm on the same day after he refused to succumb to demands for bribes made by the police personnel. It was argued that no custodial interrogation was required in the case as the co-accused were arrested and the car was recovered. In response, the Harayana government said that the accused had stolen the vehicle from the police station in the early hours of October 5, and that there were CCTV visuals of the incident. There is no need to grant the accused anticipatory bail, the State maintained. In the order passed on November 21, the Court agreed and said that there was no reason to extend the concession of anticipatory bail to the accused. Accordingly, the accused man's plea was dismissed. Advocate Ajay Kumar Dahiya represented the accused/ petitioner. Additional Advocate General Amit Sahni represented the State. [Read Order]

items.title: Delhi High Court quashes suspension of lawyer who manhandled Justice Talwant Singh during BCD election
items.summary: The Delhi High Court recently quashed the Bar Council of India (BCI's) suspension of advocate Deepak Tyagi after he tendered an unconditional apology for misbehaving with returning officer Justice Talwant Singh during the Bar Council of Delhi (BCD) elections. [ Deepak Tyagi v. Bar Council of India ]. Justice Amit Mahajan observed that the advocate gave an undertaking that he will not repeat unruly, disruptive or disrespectful behaviour inside the court premises, with any judicial officer or ex-judicial officer. Justice Amit Mahajan, Delhi High Court The BCI had placed Tyagi under interim suspension on February 27 this year over his conduct on February 22 during the Bar Council of Delhi elections. Tyagi was suspended from practicing before court, appearing or participating as an advocate during the pendency of the disciplinary proceedings. As per the allegations, on the polling day, Justice Singh proceeded towards the entry gate of the Delhi High Court after receiving complaints regarding violations of the Model Code of Conduct. At this time, Tyagi attempted to manhandle him and instigated a crowd of lawyers and raised slogans against the election machinery. The action was taken after the BCI received a suo motu complaint from the Special Committee of the BCD regarding the incident. "Any misbehaviour with, attempted manhandling of, intimidation of, or interference with the Returning Officer or the election process during a statutory Bar election strikes at the dignity of the legal profession and the integrity of the electoral process. Such conduct, if established, would amount to grave professional and other misconduct under the Advocates Act, 1961 and the Bar Council of India Rules," the Bar body said. Justice Talwant Singh Tyagi gave an express undertaking to the Court stating that he has tendered an unconditional apology for his conduct and that he has also apologised to Justice Singh, who accepted the same. The Court stated that no purpose would be served by continuing the suspension order and disciplinary action against the advocate. It thus quashed the BCI's suspension order. Advocates Sanjay Gupta, Surya Pratap Singh Chauhan, Shubhangam Thakur and Manoj Gupta represented Tyagi, who also appeared in person. Advocates Preet Pal Singh and Virat Raj Mishra appeared for BCI. items.summary: At Dubai Arbitration Week this November, the Registrar of the Dubai International Arbitration Centre (“DIAC”) is reported to have told a panel on India–UAE trade that a draft of the notification the corridor has been waiting for has been prepared. He meant the notification under Section 44(b) of India’s Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (“the Act”). Without it, an award made in Dubai or Abu Dhabi is not a “foreign award” in India and cannot be enforced there, as an award from London, Singapore or Moscow can. That India should issue it has been argued often and well. We take that case as made. Our interest is in three matters the debate tends to pass over: what the award-holder is left with today, how the question looks from New Delhi, and what to do with a Dubai clause in the meantime. A gap in the list, not a verdict on the UAE Section 44 of the Act asks two things of a foreign award. It must arise from an arbitration agreement to which the New York Convention applies, and be made in a territory that the Central Government, “ being satisfied that reciprocal provisions have been made ”, has notified in the Official Gazette. India has notified about 50 of the Convention’s 172 parties. Kuwait is on the list. So are Egypt, Nigeria, Ghana and Mauritius. Russia is covered by a 1972 notification of the USSR, which the Supreme Court has held, in a case on an award made in Ukraine, to survive the Soviet break-up. The UAE, which acceded to the Convention in 2006 without reservation, is absent. A Russian seller and an Indian buyer who choose Dubai as neutral ground will obtain an award that would have travelled to India more easily from Moscow. The explanation is administrative. Most of the list was settled by 1983, and since 1996 the Government has added six States. What the award-holder is left with With Part II of the Act closed, the usual advice is to have the award ratified by a UAE court and execute the resulting judgment in India under Section 44A of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (“CPC”). India notified the UAE for court decrees in January 2020 and named the DIFC and ADGM Courts among its superior courts. The route is less secure than it looks. Explanation 2 to Section 44A provides that a “decree” shall “in no case include an arbitration award”, even one enforceable as a decree or judgment. items.summary: The Delhi High Court has quashed criminal defamation proceedings initiated against Senior Advocate and former Biju Janata Dal (BJD) Member of Parliament Pinaki Misra for calling a lawyer a “crook”. In an order passed on November 17, Justice Sachin Datta observed that the complainant, advocate Siddhartha Singh, had failed to show that Misra's statement lowered his reputation in the estimation of others. The Court allowed Misra' plea and set aside the summoning order passed by a trial court in April 2019 as well as the complaint filed by Singh. "It is also noticed that the impugned order does not consider the context in which the words were allegedly used by the petitioner and the dismissal of the complaint by the Bar Council of Delhi," the Court said. The case arose from an August 2018 report published by The Economic Times about a complaint filed by Singh before the Bar Council of Delhi, alleging professional misconduct by Misra over a conflict of interest. At the time, Misra was a Lok Sabha MP and chairperson of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Urban Development. Singh had objected to Misra appearing for power distribution companies before the National Green Tribunal, claiming that the committee chaired by him had made adverse recommendations against the companies. The newspaper report quoted Misra as allegedly calling Singh a “crook”. Singh then sent a legal notice to Misra seeking an unconditional apology before filing the criminal defamation complaint. After considering the case, Justice Datta noted that Singh had examined only himself as a witness before the trial court and had not named or examined anyone who had read the report or whose estimation of him had been affected. The Court also noted that the Bar Council had dismissed Singh's professional misconduct complaint in November 2018. items.title: Women in high public office does not mean equality has been achieved: Justice BV Nagarathna at Oxford
items.summary: Supreme Court Justice BV Nagarathna recently said that the presence of women in high public offices does not mean equality has been achieved across the society. She added that even a guaranteed right can be difficult to exercise in practice due to cost, delay and social consequences. "The existence of women in high public office does not establish that equality has been achieved throughout society. A woman may hold a senior position while other women remain excluded from education, employment, property, or effective legal remedies," the judge said. The judge made the comment while delivering the inaugural Cornelia Sorabji Memorial Lecture at the Oxford India Centre for Sustainable Development in Somerville College, University of Oxford, on November 18. The lecture was on the topic "The Doors She Opened: Cornelia Sorabji and the Progress of Women's Rights in India." Justice BV Nagarathna A woman may hold a senior position while other women remain excluded from education, employment, property, or effective legal remedies. The judge said the progress of women's rights cannot be measured only by the number of discriminatory provisions struck down or beneficial statutes enacted. On violence against women, she said the challenge "cannot be overcome by simply enacting more laws." She also highlighted the burden of unpaid domestic and care work and the differences among women arising from caste, class, disability, religion and region. Specifically on the legal profession, Justice Nagarathna spoke about reservation for women lawyers. "I have consistently advocated for one-third reservation for women lawyers on government panels, including those representing public sector undertakings and in the sphere of legal aid, " she said. She added that the representation must go beyond the right to enter the profession and include opportunities to represent the State, advise public institutions and participate in the exercise of legal authority. Justice BV Nagarathna, Cornelia Sorabjee lecture Concluding her address, the judge said many women in India find it difficult to pursue education or a career even when they are well qualified. items.title: Maharashtra withdraws its plea before Bombay High Court against FSSAI
items.summary: The Maharashtra government has withdrawn its petition before the Bombay High Court against the Union Health Ministry and the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) over the validity of the central food safety regulations [State of Maharashtra v. Union of India & Ors.]. The plea by the State had claimed that the regulations establishing a parallel enforcement regime and was against the Constitution. The plea was listed before a division bench of Chief Justice Mahesh C Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna on November 21. Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait M Sethna When the matter came up for hearing, Advocate General Milind Sathe informed the court that the state wished to withdraw it. As per reports, the withdrawal followed outreach from FSSAI for an out-of-court resolution. Government pleader Neha Bhide informed the court that on instructions from FDA, the petition was being withdrawn. The bench recorded the statement and allowed the withdrawal. The state Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approached the court in September alleging that the Centre and FSSAI had dismantled the decentralised framework of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. Under the Act, licensing and enforcement powers belong to State commissioners and designated officers. The petition challenged the 2011 Licensing Regulations, 2018 Recruitment Regulations and 2026 Amendment Regulations. It argued that the FSSAI CEO unlawfully created posts such as ‘Central Food Safety Officer’ and ‘Central Licensing Authority’. According to the plea, the CEO’s enforcement mandate is restricted to imported food articles, not domestic ground operations. The State also contested a May 12, 2023 FSSAI directive barring State officers from inspecting centrally licensed businesses. It claimed the online FoSCoS portal was deployed to systematically bring food businesses under central jurisdiction. The plea further challenged March 10 and March 13 notifications that revised licensing turnover thresholds without inviting prior public objections, citing a violation of Section 23 of the General Clauses Act. In its prayer, the State sought to quash the regulations, stay the 2023 directive and reclaim licensing databases for state officers. items.title: Calcutta High Court upholds murder charge against building promoter after collapse kills 15
items.summary: The Calcutta High Court on Friday upheld murder charges against a building promoter in connection with the collapse of a five-storey building being developed by him and others in 2024, which claimed fifteen lives [Md. Wasim @ Wassi v. State of West Bengal and Anr] Justice Chaitali Chatterjee Das dismissed the revision petition filed by the accused Wasim for quashing the charges framed against him by the trial court. The Court observed that altering the charges would negatively impact the trial proceedings. "This Court is of the considered view that if at this threshold stage, charge is altered and a charge for substantially lesser offence is framed there would hardly remain any scope for the prosecution to proceed effectively with the trial in respect of the gravity of the allegation and the role attributed to the petitioner, even if later found some ingredients against the petitioner for commission of grave offence", the Court observed. The Court added that the trial court would be at liberty to examine the necessary evidence and decide the ultimate fate of the prosecution case during the trial. "The Court shall, therefore, have the liberty to determine the culpability of the petitioner and the ultimate of the case upon proper appreciation of the evidences to be adduced in course of trial, " it said. The five-storey building had collapsed at Azhar Molla Bagan in Kolkata on March 18, 2024. A subsequent inspection by Kolkata Municipal Corporation revealed that the construction lacked the necessary approvals. A trial court in December 2024 charged the accused under Sections 302 (murder), 307 (attempt to murder), 427 (Mischief causing damage to the amount of fifty rupees) and 120B (criminal conspiracy) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). Challenging the framing of charges, Wasim's counsel said that though he has been charged for murder and other serious offences by the trial court, the complaint letter based on which the police conducted the investigation made no mention of any act that would form the basis of these crimes. He further argued that the element of intention or knowledge was missing in the case and thus the accused could not be tried for the offence of murder. items.title: Bombay High Court orders release of undertrial kept in jail despite bail
items.summary: The Bombay High Court recently ordered the release of an accused after finding that a magistrate had erroneously remanded him to custody for failing to attend trial proceedings while he was already in jail in another case [Hitesh Chhotalal Solanki v. State of Maharashtra] A Division Bench of Justices Sarang V Kotwal and Ranjitsinha Raja Bhonsale on November 19 set aside the non-bailable warrants issued against accused Hitesh Chhotalal Solanki on July 07 and the remand order passed on July 15 by the Judicial Magistrate First Class (JMFC), Vikhroli. “ The petitioner remains in custody though he is granted bail in both these offences. This situation needs to be corrected. The petitioner deserves to be released from custody,” the Court said. Justice SV Kotwal, Justice RR Bhonsale Solanki is facing five criminal cases across Maharashtra. At present, he has secured bail in all these cases. However, two of these cases – registered at Alandi and Pant Nagar police stations – prolonged his custody. A Sessions Court had granted him bail on May 4 in a Pant Nagar police station case. However, he continued to remain in Thane Central Prison as he was still awaiting bail in the Alandi police station case. When the Pant Nagar case came up for hearing on July 07, Solanki could not appear because of his custody in the Alandi matter. On account of his absence, the Magistrate issued an NBW. Though the judge was informed about his judicial custody in the Alandi case, Solanki was still remanded to magisterial custody. The High Court criticized this judicial oversight and observed that the magistrate had erred in issuing the NBW against Solanki though he was in custody in some other case. “ Learned JMFC was not right in ignoring the earlier bail order granted in favour of the Petitioner in connection with C.R. items.summary: The Allahabad High Court recently ordered the arrest of a man who was found recording court proceedings on his mobile phone and prohibited litigants from carrying mobile phones into courtrooms [Kuldeep Batra v State of UP and Another]. The Court also passed directions prohibiting litigants from carrying mobile phones inside courtrooms. On November 19, Justice Vikram D Chauhan found Raj Kulshrestha, a resident of Varanasi, recording the proceedings taking place in his courtroom. Kulshrestha, who was in possession of an entry pass for the advocates’ chamber and not the courtroom, could not explain the reason for recording the proceedings. The Court staff, who seized his phone, found at least three videos of court proceedings there. The Court then ordered Kulshrestha be taken into custody and produced again on November 20 at 10 am. items.title: Mumbai court rejects convicted stockbroker Ketan Parekh’s plea to travel to 9 countries for 3-month vacation
items.summary: National interest and the country's economy takes precedence, a special court in Mumbai said on Friday (November 20) while rejecting a plea by convicted stockbroker Ketan Parekh seeking permission to travel abroad for 91 days [Ketan Parekh v. SEBI]. The special SEBI court observed that allowing a three-month long travel approval for overseas trip would enable Parekh, who was behind the 2000-2001 securities scam, to engage in further violations of securities laws. “It would not be expedient in the national interest and economy of the country to permit the applicant/accused to travel abroad for a longer period of three months. The possibility of applicant/accused indulging such unlawful activity in contravention to the securities law can not be ruled out if such, blanket permission for a period of three months is granted to the applicant/accused,” SEBI special judge RM Jadhav observed. Parekh approached the court seeking permission to visit Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, the UAE, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Switzerland for a family vacation without furnishing any additional security deposit. This proposed trip was scheduled to last 91 days, spanning from December 20 to March 20. SEBI opposed the plea, submitting that Parekh had previously misused travel liberties to orchestrate front-running activities using non-public information of a large client. The regulator pointed out that Parekh had not complied with a January 2, 2025 order of a Whole Time Member (WTM) directing the deposit of ₹27 crore in wrongful gains. This had also prompted SEBI to initiate fresh prosecution under securities laws It argued that the investigation was ongoing and Parekh's presence was necessary for hearings prior to taking cognizance and passing a final order. Judge Jadhav concurred with the prosecution on the risks of granting a blanket travel approval. "Granting permission for traveling abroad for such a long period for 91 days would provide him the platform to commit identical activities in violation of the securities laws," the judge said. The Court also rejected Parekh's reliance on earlier High Court precedents, noting that those cases involved brief overseas trips lasting between six and twenty days. Accordingly, the Court rejected Parekh’s application as devoid of merits and substance. Advocate Burzin Bharucha appeared for Parekh. Special public prosecutor Anubha Rastogi appeared for SEBI. items.title: Mumbai court grants anticipatory bail to Muslim man in city's first anti-conversion law case
items.summary: A Mumbai sessions court on November 20 granted anticipatory bail to a Muslim man booked under the newly enacted Maharashtra Freedom of Religion Act, 2026, for allegedly forcing his Hindu wife to convert to Islam. This case marks the first arrest in Mumbai and possibly the first anticipatory bail application across Maharashtra under the anti-conversion law. Additional Sessions Judge PA Sane of the City Civil and Sessions Court at Dindoshi in Mumbai passed the order after the Hindu woman's mother lodged a complaint alleging unlawful religious conversion. During the hearing, the complainant and prosecution relied on a wedding invitation card pairing a Muslim name with the Hindu woman's identity, alongside a photograph showing her in a burkha. The court noted that the couple had already registered a civil marriage under the Special Marriage Act on October 16 following prior statutory notice. Further, a register seized by police from a Maulavi contained no entry confirming that a religious Nikah ceremony had taken place. The Hindu woman also appeared personally before the Court and confirmed that she married voluntarily without any force, coercion, threat or inducement. In the order, Judge Sane questioned whether merely quoting a Muslim name on an invitation card proves conversion when no Nikah record exists. “The performance of the Nikah is not coming on record. So far as alleged photograph and wearing burkha will not be the sole ground to believe that daughter (of the complainant) has converted to Islam,” the order states. The judge found no ingredients to justify the allegation of unlawful inducement. “As there is a love relationship between them since the pandemic situation, apparently it is seen that both are the adults and it is difficult to believe that any of the ingredients of Section 3 (conversion by coercion or fraud) are put into motion,” the judge noted. Accordingly, the Court concluded that custodial interrogation was not required and granted pre-arrest bail to the accused-husband on a personal bond of ₹50,000. Advocate Karim Pathan, Fazal Shaikh and PP Tiwaris appeared for husband. Additional public prosecutor RS Kanojia appeared for State. Advocate Abhishek Dubey appeared for complainant. items.title: Allahabad High Court Bar Association to impose ₹5,000 fine on advocates recording reels inside court premises
items.summary: The Allahabad High Court Bar Association has announced that it will impose a ₹5,000 fine on advocates who take photographs or record videos or reels inside the court premises, including the courtrooms and corridors of the High Court. In a notice circulated by the Bar President CP Upadhyaya on November 18, the Bar Association said, "All respected advocates are hereby informed that making videos/reels and taking photographs inside the premises, courtrooms, and corridors of the Hon'ble High Court is strictly prohibited. If any advocate or any other person is caught committing such an act inside the premises, they will have to immediately deposit a fine of Rs. 5,000/- in the office of the High Court Bar Association, Allahabad." The Bar Association said that disciplinary action will also be initiated against such advocates, and warned them of the termination of their membership. "Therefore, all respected advocates are appealed not to engage in such acts that tarnish the image of this profession," it said in the notice. Social media use by advocates in connection with judicial proceedings, as well as the filming of videos inside court premises, has come under increased scrutiny in recent times. Allahabad High Court itself in a recent judicial order impressed upon lawyers to focus on building their careers rather than generating likes on social media . In 2025, the Supreme Court banned photography and videography inside its high-security zone and warned that the violators will face strict consequences. In June this year, the Kerala High Court Advocates Association (KHCAA) also warned its members of disciplinary action for creating and sharing videos and reels from within and around the High Court premises. items.title: US court sentences Indian national Nikhil Gupta to 19 years in jail for plot to kill Gurpatwant Pannun
items.summary: A United States Court on Friday sentenced Indian National Nikhil Gupta to 19 years and 7 months in jail for his involvement in a plot to assassinate Sikh separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in America. Judge Victor Marrero of the Southern District of New York passed the order. Nikhil Gupta is accused of orchestrating a contract killing of US-based Sikh separatist leader and lawyer Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York in 2023. According to the US Department of Justice (DOJ), Gupta was recruited in May 2023 by Vikash Yadav, an Indian government employee who allegedly worked with him to arrange Pannun's assassination. Prosecutors alleged that Gupta approached a criminal associate for help in hiring a contract killer. However, the associate was actually a confidential source working with the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), who introduced Gupta to an undercover DEA officer posing as a hitman. The indictment alleged that Yadav agreed to pay $100,000 for the killing and that an associate delivered an advance payment of $15,000 on June 9, 2023. Gupta allegedly provided the purported hitman with Pannun's personal details, including his New York address, telephone numbers and daily routine, along with surveillance photographs. The alleged killing was to be carried out after Prime Minister Narendra Modi's state visit to the US in June 2023. However, following the killing of Khalistani separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada on June 18, 2023, Gupta allegedly told the undercover officer that there was no longer any need to wait to carry out the killing. Gupta was arrested in the Czech Republic on June 30, 2023, at the request of US authorities and extradited to the US in June 2024. He initially denied the charges but pleaded guilty to all three counts -- murder for hire, conspiracy to commit murder for hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering -- on February 13, 2026. items.title: Sabarimala: Up to Rs 5,000 fine for discarding clothes, waste in Pamba river
items.summary: The Sabarimala season is here, drawing lakhs of devotees to Sabarimala this month, the Pampa River is once again drowning in non-biodegradable garbage at the Pampa and Triveni bathing ghats. Despite multi-language warning boards put up by the government, thousands of pilgrims are ignoring the rules and dumping synthetic clothes, plastic wrappers, and used tissues straight into the water under the guise of Vastra Danam . Vastra Danam is a ritual followed by pilgrims in which devotees abandon their worn clothes in the river, believing it washes away their past sins. The Travancore Devaswom Board assigned Clean Kerala Company Ltd (CKCL) and 30 sanitation workers; however, persistent delays in clearing the ghats have resulted in wet piles of nylon and polyester choking the riverbed. What starts out every morning as a customary dip before the forest walk swiftly devolves into a dense tangle of floating trash and abandoned clothing. As footfall climbs higher each day of the current season, the gap between pilgrim numbers and waste collection is leaving the river basin visibly suffocated. Unless enforcement tightens on the ground right now, the holy waters meant to cleanse devotees will remain buried under their own waste. Clothes all thrown overboard are reduced to a heap; the used tissues, plastics, and bits of floating debris all turn stark. What was initially an act of ritual cleansing is going to turn messy very quickly along this belt of forest. When the community attempts to explain the mess or minimize the impact on the environment, critical voices are the first to take issue with how the issue is being defined. "Any other denotation of that word is just the projection of your classist and racist perspective," said Aaron Philp, journalist. He referred to efforts to dismiss the damage and lessen the real price the river and community paid. The rituals at the riverbank The most abominable practice along the banks is Vastra Danam where people abandon their used clothes in the water. The misconception of abandoning clothes ( Vastra Danam ) in the Pampa gained momentum in the late 1990s and early 2000s among pilgrims that throwing away your clothes after a dip helps you throw away bad luck, sick health, and old sins. The locals note that the river used to have a certain fragrance in the mornings when the faithful would take a dip in the river. items.title: Commission seeks evidence from UP CM Yogi on claim of 1.27 crore missing Hindu voters
items.summary: An independent commission comprising five retired judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts has written to Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, seeking supporting material and data for his reported claim that 1.27 crore Hindus were excluded from the state's electoral rolls during the Election Commission of India's (ECI) Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise. In a letter dated November 21, the Independent Commission on SIR, proposed by the Lawyers' Association for Constitution (LAFC), said Yogi Adityanath's statement was directly relevant to its mandate of examining whether eligible voters had been unfairly removed from electoral rolls during the revision exercise. items.title: Rohingya in Bangladesh welcome UN court's genocide verdict but say they want to go home to Myanmar
items.summary: By Shamimul Islam Faisal COX’S BAZAR, Bangladesh (AP) — Hundreds of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh sat in front of a big screen at their sprawling camp in Cox’s Bazar, watching the news from the Netherlands, where the U.N.'s top court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation. For many, the historic verdict on Thursday represented a “small victory” — offering a glimmer of hope that someday they would be able to return safely to their homes in Myanmar, across the border from Bangladesh . Only then, some said, will they be “fully satisfied.” It was a landmark judgment, finding Myanmar responsible for the crime against the country’s ethnic Rohingya — the first time the court ruled that a state committed genocide. The Hague-based International Court of Justice also ordered Myanmar’s military-supported government to allow the Rohingya to return home safely, pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide. But it remains to be seen how much of the ruling can be implemented. The court’s rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce them beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council. Myanmar’s government on Friday dismissed the ruling as “unfair.” Bangladesh Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman, who is also president of the U.N. General Assembly, went to Cox’s Bazar on Friday to tell Rohingyas who fled the genocide in Myanmar that “at this historic moment” there must be action, his U.N. spokesperson said. Suspects must be prosecuted, Rohingya must be able to return to Myanmar voluntarily and safely, they must receive reparations and Myanmar’s government must ensure there will never be another genocide, Rahman said, according to spokesperson Melissa Summers. items.title: Rights groups urge sanctions after top UN court finds Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
items.summary: By Edith M. Lederer Rights groups are calling for military and economic sanctions against Myanmar after the United Nations' highest court, in the first ruling of its kind, determined that its government committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation. The International Court of Justice has no power to enforce Thursday's ruling , which orders Myanmar’s military-supported government to allow those who fled the violence to return home safely, to pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide. Myanmar’s government has denied committing genocide, claiming it acted against insurgents, and is considered unlikely to fulfill any of the court’s demands. President Min Aung Hlaing, the former military leader, was in charge of the 2017 operation. The court said evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 100,000 Rohingya. Khine Khine Soe, the president's spokeswoman, noted the International Court of Justice decision handed down Thursday had been the result of a nine-to-six vote of the judges. “Not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” she told reporters in the capital Naypyitaw. “So it was not a decision made unanimously. I would say that it was unfair.” While the World Court’s rulings are final and legally binding, it has no recourse beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council. items.title: The history of the persecution of Myanmar’s Rohingya
items.summary: Some 420,000 Rohingya Muslims, a religious and ethnic minority community in Myanmar, have fled to neighboring Bangladesh since August this year. The United Nations has called the Rohingya the world’s most persecuted minority group and described the atrocities by Myanmar’s authorities as “ ethnic cleansing ,” whereby one group removes another ethnic or religious community through violence. But the persecution of the Rohingya is not new. My research on the Rohingya Muslim experience in Myanmar shows that this pattern of persecution goes back to 1948 – the year when the country achieved independence from their British colonizers. Here is their brief history. The legacy of colonialism The British ruled Myanmar (then Burma) for over a century, beginning with a series of wars in 1824 . Colonial policies encouraged migrant labor in order to increase rice cultivation and profits. Many Rohingya entered Myanmar as part of these policies in the 17th century. According to census records , between 1871 to 1911, the Muslim population tripled. The British also promised the Rohingya separate land – a “ Muslim National Area ” – in exchange for support. During the Second World War , for example, the Rohingya sided with the British while Myanmar’s nationalists supported the Japanese. Following the war, the British rewarded the Rohingya with prestigious government posts. However, they were not given an autonomous state. In 1948, when Myanmar achieved independence from the British, violent conflicts broke out among various segments of its more than one hundred ethnic and racial groups. Decades-long persecution After independence, the Rohingya asked for the promised autonomous state, but officials rejected their request. Calling them foreigners, they also denied them citizenship. These animosities continued to grow. Many in Myanmar saw the Rohingya as having benefited from colonial rule. A nationalist movement and Buddhist religious revival further contributed to the growing hatred. In 1950, some Rohingya staged a rebellion against the policies of the Myanmar government. They demanded citizenship; they also asked for the state that had been promised them. Ultimately the army crushed the resistance movement. Where Rohingyas live The majority of Rohingyas live in the Rakhine state in Myanmar. items.title: Myanmar genocide ruling is a watershed moment in international justice – with huge ramifications for other cases
items.summary: The International Court of Justice’s historic ruling of genocide against Myanmar on Nov. 19, 2026, will have significant consequences for the parties involved in the case – and potentially some who are not. The Hague’s highly anticipated judgment in Gambia v. Myanmar is a major victory for Gambia, the tiny west African nation that filed a complaint with the court against Myanmar in 2019. It is also a major moment of accountability for the military leadership of Myanmar. But as an expert in genocide and mass atrocity prevention, I believe the ruling goes far beyond these nations. Indeed, it is also a watershed moment for international legal justice that is bound to have important effects on the court’s other ongoing genocide cases, particularly the case of South Africa v. Israel . Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar on Nov. What the court ruled Gambia’s case focused on actions that Myanmar’s military government called “clearance operations” in the course of its decades-long violent persecution of the country’s Muslim Rohingya minority . The Tatmadaw , as the Myanmar military is known, justified these actions as a counterinsurgency operation. Yet in the course of those attacks, soldiers were found to have destroyed hundreds of Rohingya villages , and to have committed widespread rapes, torture and summary killings. While the precise death toll of the 2017 attacks may never be known, at least 10,000 Rohingya civilians are thought to have died , and roughly 750,000 Rohingya fled to neighboring Bangladesh. There they joined other Rohingya in what is now the world’s largest refugee camp of over 1.2 million people, comprised of those who had already fled years of the Myanmar government’s persecution and attacks. The court’s ruling that the Tatmadaw’s attacks amounted to genocide rested on its interpretation of the crime of genocide in the 1948 U.N. Genocide Convention , the first major international treaty approved by the United Nations General Assembly. For an attack to be genocidal, it must be directed against an ethnic, religious, racial or national group, and must include at least one of five prohibited acts: killing members of a group; inflicting serious physical or mental harm on members; deliberately inflicting conditions calculated to bring about its destruction; imposing measures intended to prevent births; or forcibly transferring children from the group. items.title: Cop31: Why the UN climate summit ended in victory for fossil fuel producing nations
items.summary: The UN’s annual two-week climate summit, Cop31 , has ended in failure. Countries could not find consensus on a final agreement. It is the first such failure in more than 20 years. The summit started relatively smoothly. In fact, the conference agenda was adopted within a few hours on day one, as country parties found nothing objectionable. At the time, this event looked like it might be smooth sailing: another summit simply focused on implementing policies agreed in previous years. But week two became explosive. First, the draft agreement – which if adopted would have been known as the Antalya Accords – conceded that we have failed to keep global temperature rise below 1.5˚C and that the world is entering a period of “overshoot” . Second, oil and gas producing nations fought to keep the root cause of climate change – namely fossil fuels – out of any deal. And they succeeded, as the agreement fell through. The frustration felt by many was summed up on day ten (November 19) by Panamanian environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro, who said: “While we listen to endless oratory, the planet is being destroyed.” The country’s delegation then said enough is enough – they were not about to put their name to an outcome that does not adequately address the crisis. We are climate experts at UCL who have written about the outcome of these summits for The Conversation since Cop26 in Glasgow , and we were in Antalya this year too. Here’s why we think this year’s summit failed. Disagreement over ‘fossil fuels’ caused the collapse Every Cop meeting since 2003 has resulted in a global agreement. This year, however, countries failed to reach consensus on a final deal, after negotiations broke down over whether to explicitly address fossil fuels. Inside the negotiation rooms at Cop31 in Turkey. The draft agreement presented to the summit for approval omitted any mention of fossil fuels, after pressure from oil, gas and coal producing nations led by Saudi Arabia. The EU, Panama and many vulnerable island nations refused to agree to any text that did not explicitly address them. This disagreement ultimately prevented the summit from reaching consensus. This has been the modus operandi of these summits – they start with a more ambitious draft text that gets weakened as it comes closer to adoption. items.title: Going to the park once a week or more has a measurable impact on a child’s mental health – new study
items.summary: Child mental health issues have been rising in the UK over the last decade . This was exacerbated by the COVID pandemic and continues to be a concern, particularly around issues such as sedentary lifestyles and excessive screen time. In a new study , colleagues and I have found that visiting a local park regularly had a measurable impact on child mental health . Throughout childhood and through adolescence, children are developing their social and emotional skills. This social-emotional development provides the foundation for good mental health. Failing to reach typical milestones such as developing social skills and friendships provides an indication of a child’s current mental health, as well as their mental health in later life. This means that finding ways to facilitate and encourage healthy social-emotional development is a way to improve child mental health and give them the foundation for good mental health throughout their lives. Having green and natural spaces close to people’s homes is one factor which previous studies have shown is linked with improved child mental health. These spaces are thought to improve child mental health by encouraging healthy behaviour. For example, they encourage physical activity, socialising and imaginative and adventurous play. Research suggests that being in natural spaces can have restorative and stress-reducing effects for both children and adults . Much of the research related to green spaces and child mental health has been cross-sectional study designs. This means that the study measurements are taken at a single point in time, rather than following children over time. While these studies are good at discovering factors which are linked to each other, such as natural spaces and child mental health, they cannot determine whether it was the natural space, or other factors that impacted child mental health. These studies also typically measure residential proximity to green and natural spaces, rather than measuring how often children are actually taken to these spaces. What we did in our study For our study , we chose to focus on visiting parks, as we thought this was likely to enable many of the ways that research has suggested green and natural spaces could improve mental health. items.title: How your body clock affects your mental health and ways to keep it in sync
items.summary: Ever wondered why a bad night’s sleep can leave you irritable, anxious or sad? Poor sleep affects our emotions, but its timing also plays a role. Our circadian rhythms are nearly 24-hour cycles that regulate alertness, hormones, body temperature and digestion. Deep inside the brain, a cluster of nerve cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) acts as the body’s master clock. It uses light signals from the eyes to coordinate clocks in other organs, including the brain, liver, heart and gut. When daily routines fall out of sync with this clock, mood can suffer. Research suggests circadian disruption may contribute to mental health challenges. Our internal clock helps regulate hormones, including melatonin and cortisol. Melatonin helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle. Levels stay low during the day, rise in the evening as darkness falls (signalling to the brain that it is time to rest), peak in the middle of the night, and drop off in the morning. Cortisol, which helps us respond to stress, typically rises towards morning. These changes prepare the body for activity and rest, while influencing emotional wellbeing. In a 2024 laboratory study , my colleagues and I investigated whether our internal clocks influence mood independently of everyday activities. We studied 19 healthy adults over 32 hours, measuring mood while minimising changes in their surroundings and behaviour. We found that anxiety-like and depression-like mood were highest at around 8am to 9am, while participants reported greater mental fatigue and lower physical comfort between approximately 6am and 8am. These patterns were linked to their internal biological clocks, suggesting that mood can fluctuate according to biological time, independently of everyday routines. Circadian disruption has also been linked to depression and bipolar disorder, a condition involving episodes of depression and elevated or irritable mood. The relationship also works in both directions. Mental health difficulties can disrupt sleep and circadian rhythms, potentially creating a cycle in which low quality sleep and psychological distress reinforce one another. items.title: Rasa Theatre’s Many A Thousand Years ponders on existential dread and the ache of waiting
items.summary: Many A Thousand Years (English) Night after night, when the curtains fall on their performances, two actors meet near a rock and wait. Nothing happens, nobody comes, nobody goes; it's awful. As it was for Vladimir and Estragon in Waiting for Godot , so it is for Mano and Gomi in Many A Thousand Years . Except, there is no Godot to look forward to, even if in vain. The fourth major production by Kochi-based Rasa Theatre Collective, Many A Thousand Years attempts to explore the ‘waiting’ that is central to human existence, inspired by Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot. It is written by Aparna Ashok and directed by Rahul Thomas. Rahul plays Mano, a theatre actor who transforms into Hamlet on stage, seeking an answer to the centuries-old question: to be or not to be? Each night, as Mano washes off his makeup and removes his costumes, he is joined by another actor, Gomi, played by Abraham Vadakkan. Day in and day out, Gomi plays Bhima, who, with a swing of his mace, breaks Duryodhana’s thigh in the Mahabharata . The audience erupts in applause, the curtains fall, and Gomi resumes the wait for the next day. Monotony is the norm of their lives. The play progresses through several nights during which the same two actors wait at the same spot and discuss the same things. One night becomes indistinguishable from the next, and neither of them seem to know what they are waiting for. It is absurd theatre, and so the dialogues and gestures are bound to be repetitive and illogical. The play makes an attempt to lay bare the psyche of the artist who craves both adulation and meaning. Gomi revels in the appreciation his craft receives, hungers for more, and seems aware that he is larger than himself when playing Bhima on stage. Even when off stage, he refuses to take off a bangle that is part of his Bhima costume. Mano seems to be chasing a perfection that is just beyond reach when he is shown trying different modulations for the same line or looking for a lost hat that was perfect for him. The metatheatrical elements are not limited to the existential questions raised by the actors played by actors. The ‘stage’ leaves them notes, asking them to ‘Try again' or ‘Prepare’.
